cards.title: Can I stay past the winter season, or all summer?
cards.text: You can, but few people do. The long-term season ends April 15. After that an LTVA allows 14 days in any 28, and the free areas keep their 14-day limit. The real limit is the heat: summer days run well over 100 degrees and it is hard to live here without air conditioning, which means a hookup site in an RV park or a big generator and the fuel to run it. Most campers head north or up to higher country by late April and come back in the fall.

cards.title: What happens if I have a medical emergency in the desert?
cards.text: Call 911 and give your GPS coordinates, the nearest highway milepost and a landmark, because a campsite has no address. The Blythe emergency room is open but does not handle trauma or other advanced care; serious cases are often flown by helicopter to Palm Springs or Phoenix. Some campers carry an air-ambulance membership for that reason.

cards.title: How do I keep awnings, canopies and solar panels from blowing away?
cards.text: Pull the awning in before you leave camp or go to bed, lay portable panels flat, and hold canopies with heavy spiral ground stakes and ratchet straps. Thin tent pegs pull out of sandy ground.

cards.title: Are campfires allowed right now?
cards.text: It depends on the current BLM fire restrictions, so check before you light one. Do not burn pallets with nails or trash, and drown the fire until it is cold to the touch.

cards.title: What if my rig breaks down and I cannot move before my 14 days are up?
cards.text: Call the BLM Yuma Field Office at (928) 317-3200 or tell a camp host right away, and keep the paperwork from your mechanic. Ask them what they will allow; do not just stay.

cards.title: How do I get cholla off my dog?
cards.text: Carry a comb and needle-nose pliers on every walk. Flick the cholla ball away with the comb and pull leftover spines with the pliers. Never grab it with bare fingers.

cards.title: Are coyotes a danger to small dogs?
cards.text: Yes, mostly at dawn, dusk and night. Keep small dogs on a leash and never leave them alone in an outdoor pen.

cards.title: Which days are quietest at the shows?
cards.text: Tuesday to Thursday mornings. The opening weekend of the Big Tent is the most crowded.

cards.title: How do I get emergency alerts?
cards.text: Sign up for La Paz County alerts at lapaz.gov/AlertCenter.aspx and leave Wireless Emergency Alerts turned on in your phone.

cards.title: Los Algodones: border wait, which dentist or pharmacy, and Sunday hours
cards.text: About 90 miles south via US-95 and I-8 to the Andrade Port of Entry (park on the US side in the Quechan lot for ~$6–$10 and walk across). Bring a valid U.S./Canadian passport or passport card. Most dental clinics and pharmacies are open Mon–Sat (roughly 8am–5pm), and many major clinics/pharmacies stay open Sundays in Jan–Mar; morning crossings have shorter return lines than mid-afternoon. Get written treatment plans/itemized receipts before work begins.

cards.title: Can golf carts and e-bikes run in town and on BLM land?
cards.text: Class 1–3 e-bikes are widely ridden around town, LTVAs, and graded BLM dirt roads (not permitted on non-motorized wilderness trails). Golf carts must meet Arizona street-legal equipment/registration rules to drive on public town roads—check current ordinances with Quartzsite Town Hall at (928) 927-4333 before driving one on Main St or Hwy 95.

cards.title: Who delivers water or pumps tanks at your site?
cards.text: Several mobile honey-wagon (septic pump-out) and bulk fresh-water delivery trucks circulate through La Posa, Plomosa, Scaddan Wash, and Dome Rock from November through March. Look for sandwich-board signs along Hwy 95 and Kuehn St, ask your LTVA camp host, or post a request with your camping area and GPS coordinates in the Quartzsite BLM Camping Facebook group.

cards.title: Where do you take used motor oil and empty one-pound propane canisters?
cards.text: Never put motor oil or pressurized 1-lb cylinders in regular dumpsters or vault toilets. Take used motor oil to auto parts stores in Blythe (O'Reilly or AutoZone on Hobsonway) or check with the La Paz County Transfer Station / local repair shops for current oil/hazmat acceptance. Switch to a refillable 1-lb Flame King cylinder or a 20-lb tank with an adapter hose to eliminate disposable canisters.

cards.title: Where are pickleball, a gym and the senior center?
cards.text: Holiday Palms RV Park (355 W Main St, 928-927-5666) has two lighted outdoor concrete pickleball courts with pay-to-play day access (call ahead to confirm non-guest hours/fees, or join sessions on PlayTime Scheduler). The Quartzsite Community Center / Senior Center is at 295 E Chandler St (Mon 7am–6pm, Tue–Thu 7am–2:30pm, closed 12–1pm and Fri–Sun; 928-927-4333 ext. 404) for senior lunches, social activities, and events.

cards.title: Is there a locksmith, an RV salvage yard, or storage for the summer?
cards.text: For mobile RV/auto locksmiths, call out of Blythe, Parker, or Lake Havasu City (or ask Best Auto RV & Truck Repair in town for current mobile techs). Major RV salvage yards are in Phoenix/Apache Junction and Southern California. Several fenced RV/boat storage yards operate along Hwy 95 in Quartzsite, Ehrenberg, and Blythe—reserve by February before spring departures.

cards.title: Where can I print, scan or get something notarized?
cards.text: BCM Mail & Ship (852 W Cowell St, 928-927-4213) and Moon Mountain Mail (103 S Moon Mountain Ave, 928-927-5791) handle printing, copying, and shipping; the Quartzsite Public Library (465 N Plymouth Ave) also offers public computers/printing. For notary services, call BCM Mail & Ship, Quartzsite Town Hall (465 N Plymouth Ave), or banks in Blythe.

cards.title: Do I need a permit to sell crafts or jewelry?
cards.text: Yes. Selling goods at swap meets, gem shows, or roadside markets requires renting a vendor booth from the market operator (such as Tyson Wells or Desert Gardens) plus a Town of Quartzsite business/vendor license and an Arizona Transaction Privilege Tax (TPT) license. Casual selling without permits on BLM LTVA land is prohibited.

cards.title: Is there ethanol-free gas nearby?
cards.text: Ethanol-free ('clear' / 'rec 90') gasoline is not consistently stocked at Quartzsite's main highway stations. Check stations along the Parker Strip / Lake Havasu City (popular with boaters) or call ahead before driving; most campers running generators or SxSs use fresh regular unleaded treated with fuel stabilizer (Sta-Bil).

cards.title: Does anyone deliver firewood to La Posa South?
cards.text: Independent firewood trucks frequently drive through La Posa South, Tyson Wash, and Scaddan Wash during peak winter months selling mesquite and oak bundles, or you can pick up bundles in town at Desperado's and Woodstock. Always burn only clean, nail-free wood in an existing fire ring or off-ground fire pit, and check BLM fire restrictions on windy days.

cards.title: Where do nomads go in summer when Quartzsite gets too hot?
cards.text: By mid-April when highs hit the 90s–100s, snowbirds migrate north or up in elevation: Flagstaff, Williams, Payson, and the White Mountains in Arizona; southern Utah (Kanab, Bryce, Moab); Colorado's high country; Lake Tahoe/Eastern Sierra; or the Pacific Northwest coast.

cards.title: Where should young adults or solo campers camp?
cards.text: Solo travelers and younger vanlifers/nomads typically cluster at Scaddan Wash (free 14-day, close to town, popular with van/skoolie meetups), Dome Rock (free 14-day, scenic sunset ridge), or specific caravans inside La Posa South for safety in numbers and social events while keeping buffer space from loud generators.

cards.title: Is there a dog groomer in town?
cards.text: Mobile pet groomers occasionally set up near swap meets or RV parks during January–February; year-round brick-and-mortar groomers and boarding are in Blythe (20 miles west) and Parker (35 miles north). Keep dogs on a 6-ft leash at all times—coyotes, jumping cholla cactus, and warm-day rattlesnakes are constant hazards.

cards.title: How do you keep mice out of the rig?
cards.text: Desert packrats and mice love warm engine bays and underbellies. Seal every pipe/wiring entry hole with coarse steel wool or copper mesh plus expanding foam; never park directly against dense creosote/mesquite brush; leave hood props or LED rope lights under the chassis at night; store all pantry and pet food in hard plastic/glass bins; and use enclosed snap traps rather than loose rodenticide.

cards.title: Are tent garages allowed in the LTVA?
cards.text: Temporary pop-up shade canopies, screen rooms, and vehicle awnings are allowed while you are actively camping, provided they are well-staked against desert winds and do not damage vegetation or trench the soil. Semi-permanent structures, fencing, or leaving canopies erected on an unoccupied site for more than 5 days without BLM permission violate LTVA rules.

cards.title: Where is "The Spot" in La Posa South?
cards.text: Informal social landmarks like 'The Spot' shift slightly each season depending on where core hosts and camp circles set up along the main graded loops in La Posa South. Check the dry-erase info boards near the La Posa South host station/dump entrance or search 'The Spot' in the Quartzsite BLM Camping Facebook group for this week's pin.

cards.title: Does the LTVA permit include water, dump and trash?
cards.text: Yes. The La Posa permit ($180 for the season, $40 for 14 days) covers the dump station, water faucets and trash at La Posa South, whichever La Posa unit you camp in. Campers report the water runs on limited daytime hours, so go mid-morning.

cards.title: Where can I dump, fill water or get propane without a permit?
cards.text: RV Pit Stop at 425 N Central Blvd has propane, a dump station, filtered water and ice. Pattie's RV Park also fills propane. See Services for the full list.

cards.title: Where is the best public shower?
cards.text: Campers reported these in November 2026, so check prices before you go. Main Street Laundromat: about $11 a person for 20 minutes; it closes mid-afternoon. The truck stops (Love's, Pilot, Arco) are the cleanest, about $18, and two people can share a stall. Many RV parks sell showers for around $5. Plenty of campers use a pop-up shower tent at camp instead.

cards.title: Where do I buy firewood?
cards.text: Campers name these, with prices as last reported: Desperado's, across from Silly Al's Pizza near the post office (4 bundles for $20); Woodstock, a little farther west across from the hardware store; Terrible's gas station after dark; and Charge N Go in Ehrenberg. Some campers switch to a propane fire pit.

cards.title: Is it OK to pick up a desert tortoise?
cards.text: No. Do not startle or lift one. A frightened tortoise can empty its stored water, which can kill it. Watch from a distance and let it cross.

cards.title: How do I get mail and Amazon packages?
cards.text: The Post Office at 80 W Main holds General Delivery for 30 days (counter open Mon–Fri 9am–11am & 12pm–4pm; closed Sat–Sun, long lines in peak season). FedEx packages can be picked up/dropped off at Dollar General (925 W Main). Many campers rent a seasonal box at Moon Mountain Mail or BCM Mail & Ship, or use Amazon lockers/counters in Blythe.

cards.title: Where do social campers go, and where is it quiet?
cards.text: La Posa South is the busiest and most social. Plomosa Road and Road Runner are quieter.

cards.title: Can I camp in a tent or a van with no bathroom?
cards.text: Yes. In La Posa, rigs that are not self-contained must camp within 500 feet of a vault toilet. Tents are welcome in the free areas too.

cards.title: Is it OK to park in a wash?
cards.text: No. Overnight camping in desert washes is against the rules in La Posa, and it is dangerous everywhere. See the Washes section.

cards.title: What is going on this week?
cards.text: The Shows tab has the big show dates. For potlucks, music and meetups, the Facebook groups listed under Town are where campers post them.

cards.title: Can I drive a side-by-side or UTV in town?
cards.text: Yes, once it is registered street-legal in Arizona. That means title, registration with a plate on the rear, insurance, the OHV decal, a brake and brake light, headlights and taillights, and a red rear reflector. Eye protection is required on streets and highways. Street-legal machines can use roads other than interstates. The town traffic code adds no off-road vehicle restrictions, so state law applies. Golf carts are a separate question; ask Town Hall.

cards.title: Do I need an Arizona OHV decal?
cards.text: Every ATV, UTV or side-by-side of 2,500 pounds or less needs one, about $25 a year, and that includes visitors from other states. A basic OHV education course is now required before you can buy it. With the decal alone you are limited to trails and unmaintained roads; many graded dirt roads count as maintained and need street-legal registration. All machines need a muffler, a spark arrestor and lights at night, and riders under 18 must wear a helmet.

cards.title: Do I need a reservation for the LTVA?
cards.text: No. Just show up; there are no reservations or assigned sites. Buy the permit and vehicle sticker at the entrance, then camp anywhere inside. One permit covers every La Posa area. The boundaries are marked only by fence posts a few hundred feet apart, and rangers move people who camp outside them.

cards.title: Do I need a pass for the free 14-day areas?
cards.text: Camp hosts at the entrances hand out free date cards. Campers report the Hi Jolly host does not ask for one for a night or two. Hosts also warn pet owners about the resident coyotes.

cards.title: How do I pick a good spot?
cards.text: Never in a wash. Stay back from the roads (dust) and from the dump, trash and water stations (flies). Avoid tucking deep into brush. Spend a night or two before you set up fully, and listen for generators, music, dogs and roosters. After summer storms, watch for soft spots and washouts on LTVA roads. No fireworks in the LTVAs.

cards.title: How do I avoid the dump and water lines?
cards.text: At La Posa South the station runs roughly 8 or 9 am to 4 pm, and the water is on a timer. Lines are worst from December to March, in the morning as people leave and late afternoon as they arrive; midweek afternoons are best. Campers also use a portable waste tote, a water bladder or 5-gallon jugs, or a mobile tank-pumping service that comes to your site.

cards.title: When does the season end?
cards.text: LTVA long-term permits run September 15 to April 15. The free areas keep their 14-day limit all year. Most snowbirds leave in April when the heat arrives.

cards.title: Are there rattlesnakes in winter?
cards.text: Yes, on warm days. Campers photographed one near Dome Rock this fall. Watch where dogs sniff and carry a light after dark.

cards.title: Where is the nearest supermarket, Walmart or real hardware store?
cards.text: Blythe, 20 miles west on I-10, has Albertsons, Smart & Final, Grocery Outlet and Ace Hardware, plus a dump station for the same trip. Walmart is in Parker, north on Hwy 95. Quartzsite itself has small groceries, dollar stores and Big Market for hardware. Herb's Hardware has closed.

cards.title: Do I need to worry about snakes and scorpions?
cards.text: They are here, and small rattlesnakes are as dangerous as big ones. Residents posted a young diamondback this month. Keep doors and screens shut, shake out shoes, use a light at night and keep dogs close.

cards.title: Where can I rockhound besides Crystal Hill?
cards.text: Most people miss the Hauser Geode Beds and the Wiley's Well district west of Blythe: geodes, thundereggs, agate and fire agate. See Rockhounding.

cards.title: Is there a dentist?
cards.text: Not in Quartzsite itself. Blythe has several, listed under Dentists in Services. Many snowbirds go to Los Algodones, Mexico, for major work.

cards.title: Where do I take my trash?
cards.text: LTVA permit holders use the dumpsters in La Posa. Otherwise the county transfer station north of town is free, but only open some days. See Services.

cards.title: Which phone carrier works?
cards.text: Signal is fine almost everywhere. The trouble is congestion in January, when campers report full bars and no service; many say Starlink is the only dependable option during the shows. Best Verizon reports: Hi Jolly (the tower is right there), La Posa South and West, Dome Rock, Plomosa Road and Scaddan. Bouse, over the hill, is much faster when Quartzsite is jammed. Open an area on the Map to see signal reports and add yours when you check in.

cards.title: Where can Amazon packages go?
cards.text: Amazon pickup counters are in Blythe and fill up in season. In town, a private mailbox is the reliable way. See Mail and packages in Services.

cards.title: Can I stay just a night or two for the show?
cards.text: Yes. The free 14-day areas need no reservation. The LTVA sells a 14-day permit if you want the dump and water.

cards.title: Who do I call about a loud party after 10pm?
cards.text: LTVA quiet hours are 10pm to 6am. Tell the camp host, or call the BLM Yuma Field Office at (928) 317-3200.

cards.title: Something was stolen. Where do I report it?
cards.text: Call the La Paz County Sheriff, and tell your neighbors so they can watch for it.

cards.title: Who fixes generators, brakes, propane and slide-outs?
cards.text: This is the most common request of all. Look under Services in the For Sale tab, or post a Wanted ad saying what you need. For tires, see Services in this guide.

cards.title: How do I get to town without a car?
cards.text: The Camel Express dial-a-ride picks up at the camping areas. See Getting around in Services.

cards.title: Is there a farmers market?
cards.text: One is listed: the Farmers Market of Quartzsite at 960 W Main St, Thursday to Saturday, 9:00am–2:00pm, late October through March. We have not confirmed this season's days, so check before you go. Produce also turns up at the swap meets.

cards.title: Where can I buy dry ice?
cards.text: Smart & Final in Blythe has it, about 20 miles west on I-10. We know of no store in Quartzsite that sells it.

cards.title: When does the LTVA season end, and what happens in summer?
cards.text: The long-term season runs September 15 to April 15. From April 16 to September 14 you can stay in an LTVA only 14 days in any 28-day period, and La Posa charges per vehicle: $10 for the day, $15 overnight, or $75 for the year. The free 14-day areas stay open all year, but it is very hot.

cards.title: Do my dogs need rabies papers to camp on BLM land?
cards.text: We found no BLM rule that asks for papers at the gate. The LTVA rules do say pets must be on a leash at all times and you must clean up after them. Carry the rabies certificate anyway: vets, groomers and boarding kennels ask for it.

cards.title: Where can a beginner look for gold?
cards.text: On BLM land you may prospect with hand tools, a pan or a metal detector if you barely disturb the surface. Not on someone else's mining claim without permission, and not on Arizona State Trust land. Much of the ground near town is claimed, so check the claim map with the BLM first, or go out with the Quartzsite Metal Detecting Club (see Gatherings and clubs).

cards.title: My solar panels are not charging. Who can help?
cards.text: Two solar shops are listed in town, Discount Solar and Solar Bill (see Hardware and RV parts in Services). Before you go: wipe the dust off, tilt the panels south, and check that the controller shows the panels and the battery.

cards.title: My motorhome or diesel broke down. Who do I call?
cards.text: Best Auto RV & Truck Repair is the shop in town (see RV repair and towing in Services). The mobile RV techs listed there fix house systems like fridges, furnaces and plumbing, not engines. For a big diesel job, expect a tow to Blythe, Parker or Yuma.

cards.title: Who fixes RV plumbing leaks?
cards.text: A mobile RV tech. See RV repair and towing in Services, or post a Wanted ad saying what leaks and where you are camped.

cards.title: Where do I turn in for La Posa South?
cards.text: The LTVA has no street address. Enter only at the signed access roads on US-95 south of town; the La Posa pins on the Map show each entrance, and Directions will take you there.

cards.title: How busy is it right now at Plomosa or La Posa?
cards.text: That changes week to week, so ask in Alerts. Someone camped there can answer.

cards.title: Dome Rock: how it works
cards.text: Sign in with the camp host near the Exit 17 end for your free 14-day stay. Stay clear of the marked gas pipeline strip; campers report being asked to move. The further west you go toward Exit 11, the quieter and hillier it gets.

cards.title: Tribal land between Dome Rock and the river
cards.text: West of the Dome Rock Mountains, toward Ehrenberg and the Colorado River, much of the desert belongs to the Colorado River Indian Tribes (CRIT). Congress returned about 16,000 acres there, the La Paz lands, to the reservation in 2005. It is not BLM land: the 14-day rule does not apply, and the Tribes set their own camping and off-road rules. Before you camp, ride or collect there, call CRIT Fish and Game in Parker at (928) 669-9285.

cards.title: Ehrenberg Sandbowl
cards.text: Free BLM camping south of I-10 Exit 1, 17 miles west. Popular with off-roaders. Not great for big rigs.

cards.title: Oxbow Recreation Area
cards.text: BLM river camping south of Ehrenberg, about $15 a night. No water or dump.

cards.title: Midland LTVA
cards.text: BLM long-term area 8 miles north of Blythe. Take Lovekin Blvd north from I-10; it becomes Midland Road. Open desert, few services. Rigs must be self-contained. Uses the same LTVA permit as La Posa.

photo.credit: Photo: BLM California, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Wiley's Well campground
cards.text: Mule Mountain LTVA, west of Blythe. I-10 Exit 222, then 9 miles south on Wiley's Well Road (the last 6 are graded dirt). Same LTVA permit as La Posa.

cards.title: Coon Hollow campground
cards.text: 3 miles past Wiley's Well on the same road. The closest camp to the Hauser Geode Beds. Bring all your water; Blythe is about 30 miles away.

cards.title: Check the road first
cards.text: BLM posted on October 15, 2026 that Wiley's Well Road was storm damaged and impassable for RVs and trailers. Check blm.gov or call (760) 833-7100 before you go.

cards.title: Boomerville
cards.text: The Escapees Boomers club circles up at Scaddan Wash in January. Ask around for this year's spot.

cards.title: Quartzfest
cards.text: Ham radio operators gather at Road Runner for a week in January, with antennas everywhere.

cards.title: "The Spot" and other nicknames
cards.text: Campers ask where named hangouts like The Spot in La Posa South are. If you know one, tap Suggest a fix below so newcomers can find it.

cards.title: Van and skoolie camps
cards.text: Van dwellers and bus conversions tend to cluster at Scaddan Wash and Dome Rock around the January gatherings.

cards.title: The rule
cards.text: In the La Posa LTVA you may not camp overnight in a desert wash. Rangers do enforce it.

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.text: Tyson Wash drains the whole La Posa Plain north through town. After rain it can run several feet deep, and the rain can fall miles away while the sky over your camp is clear.

cards.title: It happened this season
cards.text: Campers reported washes running in La Posa South, Tyson Wash and Road Runner after the storms in late October and early November 2026.

cards.title: How to spot a wash
cards.text: Loose sand or gravel in a channel, cut banks, driftwood and debris lines, and a ribbon of ironwood, palo verde and mesquite trees. The shade is tempting. Camp on the bank above it.

cards.title: Driving
cards.text: Do not drive into moving water. Twelve inches can carry off a car. Wait it out. Washes usually drop within hours.

cards.title: Hauser Geode Beds
cards.text: The one many visitors never hear about. On BLM land in California: take I-10 west past Blythe to the Wiley's Well Road exit, about 36 miles from Quartzsite, then go south past the Wiley's Well and Coon Hollow campgrounds to the signed dirt road. About an hour beyond Blythe, half of it on washboard dirt. Take a truck or high-clearance rig, a shovel and plenty of water.

cards.title: Potato Patch and Straw Beds
cards.text: Two more digging areas within a couple of miles of the Hauser beds. Same road in, so plan them as one trip.

cards.title: Wiley's Well district
cards.text: The hills and washes around the geode beds carry agate, chalcedony roses and fire agate. The Opal Hill fire agate mine is a private claim, so ask before you collect there. Fire agate also turns up outside the claim: locals say you just have to explore the surrounding hills and look. Coon Hollow campground makes a good base for a few days.

cards.title: Day-trip rock sites
cards.text: Within a day of camp: the Black Agate thunderegg area, Straw Beds, Potato Patch, North Black Hill and Cinnamon geode beds around Wiley's Well; limonite cubes in the McCoy Mountains near Blythe; tube agate at Clapp Spring in the Palo Verde Mountains; and quartz crystals in the southern Palen Mountains. The Roadrunners club runs field trips.

cards.title: Red Cloud Mine
cards.text: World-famous for orange-red wulfenite, with fluorite, willemite and calcite that glow under UV. You pay to dig the tailings. The 2026/27 season opened September 18. See redcloudmine.com before you drive.

cards.title: South Geronimo Mine
cards.text: Wulfenite, vanadinite and mimetite. Check that it is open before you go.

cards.title: Gem show buying tips
cards.text: Get to Desert Gardens by about January 8 to 10; many vendors set up in the first week and then leave for Tucson. Desert Gardens is south of I-10 and strong on slabs and rough. Tyson Wells is mostly general goods with some good rough. Bring a resale license if you have one, since some sellers are wholesale only. Prices generally run below Tucson.

cards.title: Crystal Hill
cards.text: About 11 miles away in the Kofa refuge: turn east off Hwy 95 near mile marker 95. It is the only place in Kofa where collecting is allowed. Clear and milky quartz, with some tourmaline and pyrite. Surface collecting only, no tools, and a limit of 10 specimens or 10 pounds. Camping nearby has no water and a 14-day limit in any 12 months. The town takes its name from quartz like this: the hill has produced clear crystals up to 10 inches long.

photo.credit: Photo: Farwestern Photo by Gregg M. Erickson, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Dome Rock
cards.text: West of town by the free camping area. Campers call Dome Rock Road the place to look for quartz, and the hills around Sugarloaf, 6 to 7 miles west-southwest of town, are covered with it. Walk the washes after a rain. Watch for rattlesnakes and scorpions around rock piles.

cards.title: Round Mountain and the Plomosa Mountains
cards.text: BLM hills east of town with small to medium geodes. High-clearance vehicle recommended.

cards.title: Opal Hill Mine
cards.text: Fire agate site in the Mule Mountains, near Coon Hollow campground off Wiley's Well Road. Visitors describe a pay-to-dig mine open in the cool season, reached by a high-clearance 4WD road. Find out whether it is open before you drive.

cards.title: Saddle Mountain
cards.text: BLM land near Tonopah, about 80 miles east on I-10, with petroglyphs, hiking, rockhounding and free 14-day camping. The dirt roads in are rough in places.

cards.title: Tungsten Mine and the Cinnabar Mine
cards.text: Two old workings reached by off-road trails, with a loading chute, shafts and adits still standing. Stay out of every opening.

cards.title: Tyson's Well and the Oasis Hotel site
cards.text: Charles Tyson dug the well by hand in 1864, and it became a stage stop on the Ehrenberg to Prescott road. A plaque in town marks where the Oasis Hotel stood.

cards.title: Ehrenberg Pioneer Cemetery
cards.text: The old river-town cemetery in Ehrenberg, from the steamboat days on the Colorado.

photo.credit: Photo: Marine 69-71, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Gold Eye Mine
cards.text: The best-known old mine camp near Quartzsite, tucked against the Dome Rock hills southwest of town, not far from the Dome Rock camping area. Named for the Gold Eye Lode, a gold vein found in the late 1800s. Lehre Erdman worked the claim for 63 years, until he died in 1996, and built the stone cottage that still stands without its roof. Expect stone cabins, old equipment, a lookout tower and many covered shafts. A visitor video lists the cabin at GPS 33 36.116 N, 114 17.978 W. High clearance or a side-by-side is best. Look, photograph, and leave everything where it is.

cards.title: The Potty Garden
cards.text: Part of the Gold Eye camp: a desert garden planted in old toilets. It is the photo most visitors come home with.

cards.title: Over the hills to Ehrenberg
cards.text: Riders reach Gold Eye from the river side too, taking the gas line trail and then the power line trail across the Dome Rock hills from Ehrenberg. One group took about two hours with stops. Land on the west side of the hills includes Colorado River Indian Tribes land, so check before you ride it.

cards.title: Dome Rock placers
cards.text: The old placer country on the east side of the Dome Rock Mountains, about five miles west of town along the old highway: La Cholla, Middle Camp and Oro Fino. Prospectors have dry-washed these gulches since the 1860s and some still do, and clubs hold active claims here. Expect old diggings, hand-stacked rock, prospect holes and the remains of camps.

cards.title: Gold Nugget Road
cards.text: I-10 Exit 26, east of Quartzsite in the Plomosa Mountains. The road is a stretch of the old highway along the north side of Guadalupe Mountain, with free dispersed BLM camping that campers describe as quiet, with many open spots.

cards.title: Middle Camp, La Cholla and Oro Fino
cards.text: The three named camps of the Dome Rock placers. Most of the digging was around Middle Camp Mountain. Water was so scarce that miners worked the gravel dry or packed water in from the Colorado River.

cards.title: La Paz diggings and the La Paz townsite
cards.text: Pauline Weaver panned the first gold here in January 1862, on the west side of the Dome Rock Mountains, and the rush that followed put this corner of Arizona on the map. La Paz boomed on the river, then emptied when the placers played out and people moved to Ehrenberg. The area is on Colorado River Indian Tribes land, so call CRIT Fish and Game at (928) 669-9285 before you explore.

cards.title: Yellow Dog Mine and the lonely graves
cards.text: Old cabins, mine sites and a handful of miners' graves in the hills near town. Families still made a living here in the early 1930s. Mining stopped in 1941 when the war began.

cards.title: Plomosa Mountains
cards.text: The other gold range. Placers and hard-rock mines for gold, silver, copper and lead are scattered through the Plomosas and across the La Posa Plain between the two ranges.

photo.credit: Photo: Patrick Alexander, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Dos Picachos Mine and Dripping Springs
cards.text: A ruined stone cabin, a spring in a cave and hundreds of petroglyphs, a mile past the Dos Picachos Mine. The road is steep and rutted. Four-wheel drive only.

cards.title: Mine exhibit at the Quartzsite Museum
cards.text: 161 W Main St (Wed–Sun 10am–4pm, Nov–Mar). The museum in the old Tyson's Well stage stop keeps the original assay shack from the Mariquita Mine and an exhibit on area mines, including the Cinnabar Mine south of town, Copper Bottom in the Cunningham Mountains and Farrar Gulch to the west. Ask volunteers which roads are passable this year.

cards.title: Swansea ghost town
cards.text: A copper town near Parker with about 500 people by 1909. It closed for good in 1937 and BLM now protects the ruins. The last stretch is long, rough dirt, so take a high-clearance vehicle and plenty of water.

photo.credit: Photo: BLM Arizona, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Castle Dome City
cards.text: A restored mining ghost town and museum toward Yuma, where lead and silver ore was found in 1864. Good for weathered-building photos without the rough roads.

cards.title: Big Bertha Mine
cards.text: Old mine and hiking area in the Dome Rock Mountains west of town.

cards.title: Wyatt Earp's Mine
cards.text: A small historic mine in the hills on the California side of the river, north-west of Parker. Visitors say you need a 4WD, or a walk up a sandy wash, to reach it.

cards.title: Agate and Palm Mine
cards.text: Far out in the desert north of Wenden, off Alamo Lake Road and a long dirt road. One visitor reports green onyx and palm bog in the wash and flats beside the mine.

cards.title: Quartzsite Town Park
cards.text: By the library on Plymouth Ave, open 7am to 9pm. Visitors describe a splash pad, disc golf and a skate park. Reported to have restrooms, shaded picnic ramadas, pickleball and basketball courts, walking paths and a playground. A daytime stop when you need shade.

cards.title: Quartzsite Dog Park
cards.text: A fenced off-leash area at 555 Plymouth Rd, next to Town Park, open 6am to 6pm, with separate sides for large and small dogs. Safer than the open desert, away from cholla and coyotes.

cards.title: Reader's Oasis Books
cards.text: 690 E Main St. The well-known roadside used bookstore. It may not keep regular hours, so check before you go.

cards.title: Holiday Palms RV Park
cards.text: 355 W Main St, (928) 927-5666. Pool, dances, exercise classes and pickleball. Not staying there? Call the office and ask about day use.

cards.title: Quartzsite Public Library
cards.text: 465 N Plymouth Ave, (928) 927-6593. Free Wi-Fi, public computers, printing/copying, air-conditioned reading room, book sales, and snowbird community bulletin boards. Great spot to escape afternoon wind or catch up on email when cell towers bog down.

cards.title: Quartzsite Community & Senior Center
cards.text: 295 E Chandler St, (928) 927-4333 ext. 404. Open Mon 7:00am–6:00pm, Tue–Thu 7:00am–2:30pm (closed 12–1pm; closed Fri–Sun). Hosts senior congregate meals, card games, fitness classes, and seasonal town events.

cards.title: Solar, Batteries & Winter Power Tips
cards.text: Winter sun sits low in the southern sky—tilt portable panels 45–50 degrees south and park with an unobstructed southern exposure. Afternoon dust coats panels fast; wipe them down every few days. Respect 10pm–6am quiet hours and aim generator exhaust away from neighboring rigs.

cards.title: Stargazing & Dark Sky Nights
cards.text: Once you drive 2–3 miles outside the I-10/US-95 corridor (Plomosa Road, Road Runner, or Dome Rock), Sonoran Desert winter skies are crystal clear. Bring binoculars for the Orion Nebula, Pleiades, and winter Milky Way—especially during new-moon weeks.

cards.title: Celia's Rainbow Gardens
cards.text: Eight acres of desert gardens in Quartzsite Town Park, planted in memory of Celia Winer, who died at age 8 in 1994. It includes a miniature pioneer village donated by locals.

cards.title: Camel sculpture tour
cards.text: Camel sculptures all over town honor the Army camel experiment. A free self-guided audio tour on VoiceMap is called "Quartzsite's Camels: An Arizona Sculpture Tour". The wheel-rim "Red Ghost" camel usually stands outside Gem World at 1330 W Main.

photo.credit: Photo: Gordon Leggett, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: The Red Ghost
cards.text: Local legend from the 1880s: a red camel said to roam the desert carrying a skeleton on its back.

cards.title: Roadside stops
cards.text: The World's Largest Belt Buckle, and the F-4 Phantom jets at the Freedom Garden.

cards.title: Fuel for big rigs
cards.text: Campers say the east exit (Chevron and AM/PM) and the west exit truck stop are easy to get in and out of. The mid-town Chevron is tight.

cards.title: Eating out
cards.text: Many places are seasonal and open only a few months a year, so check before you go. New this fall, campers report: Istanbul Mediterranean Grill on Main Street, and Kenicki's seasonal food cart (burgers to BBQ). For current tips, campers use the Quartzsite food groups on Facebook.

cards.title: Facebook groups campers use
cards.text: The biggest for camping questions is "Quartzsite, AZ - BLM Camping" (public, about 54,000 members). Also busy: "Quartzsite Chatter", "What's Up Quartzsite Arizona", "Quartzsite Unleashed", "Quartzsite Area Foodies", "Quartzsite and La Paz County Music Happenings", "Quartzsite Resources", and several buy, sell and trade groups.

cards.title: Good neighbor habits
cards.text: Pack out your trash and clean your fire ring. View rock art from a distance. And the advice campers repeat most: if the neighbors bother you, jacks up, wheels roll.

cards.title: Winter weather
cards.text: Days in the 60s and 70s, nights in the 40s, and dark by about 6 pm. Expect wind and dust. Locals advise against driving the desert roads at night.

cards.title: Watch and read
cards.text: The documentary "One Road to Quartzsite" (2022), and the Huell Howser "California's Gold" episode on Quartzsite (2001).

cards.title: Hi Jolly Monument
cards.text: Pyramid tomb of Hadji Ali, a camel driver for the Army camel experiment of the 1850s. In the town cemetery.

photo.credit: Photo: Marine 69-71, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Tyson's Well Stage Station Museum
cards.text: 161 W Main St, (928) 916-7985. The historic 1860s stage stop on the Ehrenberg-to-Prescott route, from when the town was called Tyson's Wells. Winter hours (Nov–Mar): Wed–Sun 10am–4pm (closed Mon–Tue). Summer hours (Apr–Oct): Thu 9am–12pm or by appointment. Free admission (donations appreciated).

photo.credit: Photo: Marine 69-71, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Clocks
cards.text: Arizona stays on Mountain Standard Time all year. If you came from California in winter, set your watch ahead an hour.

cards.title: Free camping limit
cards.text: The free BLM areas allow 14 days in any 28-day period. After that you move on or buy an LTVA permit.

cards.title: Palm Canyon, Kofa refuge
cards.text: Arizona's only native palms, about 45 California fan palms in a narrow gorge. Drive 19 miles south on Hwy 95, then about 7 miles east on Palm Canyon Road to the trailhead. It is about a half-mile walk to the overlook. A passenger car is fine in good weather. No water or services.

photo.credit: Photo: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Blythe Intaglios
cards.text: Giant figures scraped into the desert floor long ago, about 15 miles north of Blythe on US-95 in California. Six figures at three spots; the largest human figure is 171 feet long. Free, fenced by BLM, leashed dogs welcome. They are hard to make out from the ground.

photo.credit: Photo: Rsfinlayson, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: The Desert Bar, Parker
cards.text: The Nellie E Saloon: an off-grid, solar-powered Old West bar in the Buckskin Mountains, 5 miles down rough Cienega Springs Road off Hwy 95 north of Parker. Reported hours are Saturday and Sunday, noon to 6, from about early October to late April, with live music most weekends. Families and pets welcome. High clearance recommended. (928) 667-2871.

cards.title: Castle Dome Mine Museum
cards.text: A restored mining ghost town with more than 50 buildings, off Hwy 95 toward Yuma. The gravel road in runs beside Yuma Proving Ground. The Hull Mine tour is nearby.

cards.title: Cibola National Wildlife Refuge
cards.text: About 45 miles southwest (via I-10 west to Blythe, then south along the Colorado River on Neighbours Blvd / Cibola Lake Rd). Prime winter birdwatching for tens of thousands of sandhill cranes, Canada geese, snow geese, and raptors along the auto tour loop (Nov–Feb).

cards.title: Yuma Territorial Prison & Historic Downtown
cards.text: About 85 miles south via US-95. Tour the 1876 sandstone prison cells overlooking the Colorado River, walk the historic Main Street shops and restaurants, or combine with a morning walk across to Los Algodones.

photo.credit: Photo: Pretzelpaws, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Imperial National Wildlife Refuge
cards.text: About 65 miles south off US-95. Free. Colorado River wetlands, wildlife lookouts and the short Painted Desert Trail. Visitor center reported open Friday to Sunday, 10 to 4, in winter.

cards.title: Bill Williams River National Wildlife Refuge
cards.text: About 45 miles north, just past Parker. Birdwatching, level viewing areas and flat-water paddling where the river meets Lake Havasu.

cards.title: Poston Memorial Monument
cards.text: About 30 miles north near Poston. A free roadside monument to the Poston War Relocation Center, where more than 17,000 Japanese Americans were held in World War II. Paved pull-off with plaques.

cards.title: 'Ahakhav Tribal Preserve
cards.text: South of Parker, run by the Colorado River Indian Tribes. Restored wetlands, easy riverside trails, picnic ramadas and birding. Check the tribe's access rules and fees at the entrance.

cards.title: Buckskin Mountain and River Island state parks
cards.text: About 47 miles north on the Parker Strip. Riverside picnic spots, paved walks, a beach and hiking trails. azstateparks.com.

cards.title: Parker Dam
cards.text: About 50 miles north. A scenic river drive on AZ-95 to the dam overlook.

cards.title: Camp Bouse memorial, Bouse
cards.text: About 25 miles northeast. A memorial to the secret World War II tank training camp, with small-town history displays.

cards.title: Parker Strip and Lake Havasu
cards.text: River parks north of Parker, and London Bridge at Lake Havasu City, about 70 miles north.

photo.credit: Photo: Ken Lund, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Alamo Lake State Park
cards.text: A remote desert lake northeast of town for fishing and kayaking. A long drive; fuel up first.

photo.credit: Photo: duroc2006, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Yuma and Los Algodones
cards.text: About 80 miles south. Many snowbirds cross at Los Algodones for dental, glasses and prescriptions. Bring your passport.

photo.credit: Photo: Comisión Mexicana de Filmaciones, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Wahner Brooks display, Yuma Proving Ground
cards.text: Historic military vehicles on outdoor display on Imperial Dam Road, outside the post gate. A stop on the way to Yuma.

cards.title: Bouse Fisherman Intaglio
cards.text: A 30-foot ground figure of a person spearing fish. About 6 miles north of town, turn east off Hwy 95 onto Plomosa Road and drive 8 miles. A quarter-mile trail leads to the fenced site.

cards.title: Tyson Wash petroglyphs and grinding holes
cards.text: Just south of town off Hwy 95. Park before Tyson Wash; the petroglyphs are on a rocky outcrop, with caves and grinding holes on the cliff across the wash. GPS 33.61566, -114.237724.

cards.title: Dripping Springs petroglyphs
cards.text: Near Brenda: hundreds of old petroglyphs, a ruined stone cabin and an arrastre. A spring drips from a cave roof into a pool that holds water all year. About a mile past the Dos Picachos Mine on a steep, rutted road that needs 4WD. GPS 33.610599, -114.078385.

cards.title: Look, never touch
cards.text: Skin oils and chalk damage rock art, and taking or marking it is a federal crime. Photos only.

cards.title: Rock alignments off Plomosa Road
cards.text: Big fields of laid-out rock patterns, paths and squares, out toward the Sunkist trail. Nobody agrees on who made them: campers say World War II training camps, wartime navigation arrows for pilots, or decades of visitors adding rocks. One camper puts a large "dragon's tail" alignment at mile marker 2. Good from a drone. Look, and leave every rock where it is.

cards.title: Old Yuma Road petroglyphs
cards.text: Petroglyphs and grinding stones reached by e-bike or off-road. Group e-bike rides leave from the La Posa South gate and from Tyson Wash; ask in the Facebook groups for ride times.

cards.title: Kofa Queen Canyon and Skull Rock
cards.text: 3.3 miles up Palm Canyon Road, turn left on Kofa Queen Canyon Road and drive 6.8 miles to Skull Rock. High clearance required, 4WD recommended.

cards.title: Gargoyle Canyon
cards.text: Narrow slot canyons in the desert near Palo Verde, south of Blythe. Nothing is signed, so search "Gargoyle Canyon" on Google Maps for the turnoff. Visitors say to park by the highway and walk in about a quarter mile, or take a 4x4 to the canyon mouth. It narrows the farther you go. Watch for loose rock overhead, and stay out if rain is anywhere in the forecast.

cards.title: Know another one?
cards.text: Tap Suggest a fix below and it can be added here.

cards.title: Clapp Spring
cards.text: A desert spring in the Palo Verde Mountains south of Coon Hollow, known to rockhounds for the tube agate nearby. Do not count on finding water there.

cards.title: Livingston Hills
cards.text: Low hills a few miles south of Crystal Hill, off US-95 south of Quartzsite.

cards.title: Walter's Wash
cards.text: A small nature preserve near Roll, north-east of Yuma. A long day trip south.

cards.title: Kofa refuge roads
cards.text: Kofa Queen Canyon, Big Eye Mine and the Castle Dome roads are popular high-clearance trips. The refuge allows only street-legal, licensed vehicles, and only on its numbered roads.

cards.title: Dripping Springs
cards.text: A rough backcountry trip east of town to old mine sites and a spring. High clearance, and a downloaded map, are a must.

cards.title: Arizona Peace Trail
cards.text: A signed off-road loop of about 675 miles through La Paz, Mohave and Yuma counties. Quartzsite is a gateway town, with an off-road staging area (look for the red roof) where you can leave a tow vehicle. GPX files and maps: arizonapeacetrail.org/resources.

cards.title: Swansea ghost town
cards.text: A BLM-managed copper town past Bouse toward Parker: adobe and brick buildings, a railroad grade, foundations and shafts, beside the Swansea Wilderness. Mining began in 1862 and ended by 1937. High clearance, extra water, no cell service. Tell someone before you go.

photo.credit: Photo: BLM Arizona, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.title: Ehrenberg Sandbowl
cards.text: Open sand hills for riding, south of I-10 Exit 1, 17 miles west.

cards.title: Quartzsite Off-Road Atlas
cards.text: Sold by the Chamber of Commerce: 54 pages of topo maps with BLM route numbers and more than 100 points of interest with GPS, including mines, stone cabins, petroglyphs and geoglyphs. The best single map for this area.

cards.title: Hillbilly Trail
cards.text: About 29 miles through the Little Harquahala Mountains, from I-10 to near Vicksburg.

cards.title: Granite Mountain Loop and the Cone cabin
cards.text: A loop of about 7 miles around Granite Mountain just south of town. It passes the Joseph Freemont Cone cabin and workshop, with quartz set around the doors and windows and bottles built into the walls.

cards.title: Ehrenberg to Diablo Pass
cards.text: For experienced off-roaders only.

cards.title: Before you go
cards.text: Carry a full-size spare, a plug kit and compressor, a tow strap, and more water than you think you need. Tell someone your route.

cards.title: Quartzsite OHV staging area
cards.text: On Quail Trail St, just off Plymouth Ave. The in-town staging area for the Arizona Peace Trail.

cards.title: La Posa designated trails
cards.text: Primitive roads around the La Posa camping areas for high-clearance and 4WD vehicles. The BLM publishes a four-map access guide: blm.gov/arizona/public-room/map/la-posa-access-guide-map

cards.title: Quartzsite Desert Dust Run
cards.text: January 10 to 17, 2027. Jeep and side-by-side runs, hiking, and two days of seminars that include an introduction to boondocking. Details at quartzsitedesertdustrun.com.

cards.title: QIA Desert Sky Theater
cards.text: Live entertainment shows with dinner at the QIA in town.

cards.title: Frenchy's Fireside Chats
cards.text: A weekly community campfire at Tyson Wash, run by Frenchy's Open Road. The sign reads Wednesdays from 4 pm. It ran all last winter and was set up again this season.

cards.title: Rubber Tramp Rendezvous
cards.text: Van and car dwellers meet each January, in recent years at Quartzsite Town Park, with a women's gathering just before. Dates come from the Homes on Wheels Alliance.

cards.title: Escapees and Xscapers
cards.text: Escapees held a free "Party on Plomosa" in January 2026. The Xscapers Bash for working-age RVers was near Lake Havasu in 2026, not in Quartzsite.

cards.title: Quartzsite Metal Detecting Club
cards.text: Monthly meetings at the QIA building, coin hunts in Town Park and desert outings in season.

cards.title: Quartzsite Roadrunners Gem and Mineral Club
cards.text: Classes and meetings at 65 Ironwood, November to April.

cards.title: Quartzfest
cards.text: A week of ham radio on BLM land south of town each January.

cards.title: Saguaro
cards.text: The tall cactus with arms, scattered around Quartzsite and thicker toward the Kofa and Plomosa foothills. It grows slowly: a saguaro is often 50 years old or more before its first arm. White flowers open in May. Never cut, dig or damage one.

cards.title: Cholla
cards.text: Teddy bear cholla looks soft and is not. Its joints break off at a touch and the barbed spines hold on. Buckhorn and pencil cholla grow here too. Flick a joint off with a comb or pliers, never your fingers, and keep dogs leashed around them.

cards.title: Barrel cactus
cards.text: Stout and ribbed, with hooked red or yellow spines. It often leans toward the south-west, which is why some call it compass cactus. Do not cut one for water: the pulp can make you sick.

cards.title: Beavertail cactus
cards.text: Blue-gray pads with no long spines, but thousands of tiny hair-like ones that stick in skin. Bright magenta flowers in March and April.

cards.title: Hedgehog and fishhook cactus
cards.text: Small clumping cacti among the rocks. Hedgehog cactus flowers magenta in spring. Fishhook cactus is small enough to miss until you kneel on it.

cards.title: Ocotillo
cards.text: Tall whip-like canes, and not a cactus. Gray and leafless most of the year, green within days of rain, with red flower tips in spring that hummingbirds visit.

cards.title: Creosote bush
cards.text: The most common shrub here: small waxy leaves, yellow flowers, and the smell of desert rain. It can live a very long time by spreading outward in a ring.

cards.title: Palo verde
cards.text: Arizona's state tree. Green bark, tiny leaves, and a burst of yellow flowers in April. Blue palo verde grows along washes and foothill palo verde on the slopes.

cards.title: Ironwood
cards.text: Gray-green trees along the washes with lavender flowers in late spring. The wood is very dense and the trees grow slowly and live for centuries. They shelter young saguaros and many birds. Never cut one.

cards.title: Mesquite and catclaw
cards.text: Mesquite has feathery leaves and bean pods and grows along washes. Catclaw acacia is the "wait-a-minute bush": curved thorns that grab clothes and skin.

cards.title: Smoke tree
cards.text: A gray tree of sandy washes that looks like a puff of smoke from a distance. Deep blue-purple flowers in early summer.

cards.title: Brittlebush
cards.text: Silver-leaved mounds covered in yellow daisies from about February to April, on rocky slopes and road edges.

cards.title: Desert mistletoe
cards.text: The dark clumps in palo verde, ironwood and mesquite. Its berries feed phainopeplas, the glossy black crested birds that perch on top.

cards.title: California fan palm
cards.text: Arizona's only native palm grows wild in Palm Canyon in the Kofa refuge, a day trip south. See Trips and trails.

cards.title: Wildflowers
cards.text: After a wet winter the desert blooms from late February into April: desert marigold, lupine, sand verbena, desert lily and globemallow. In a dry year you may see almost none.

cards.title: Look, do not take
cards.text: Arizona's native plant law protects saguaros, most other cacti, ocotillo, ironwood, palo verde and mesquite. Digging or cutting them on public land without a permit is illegal. Photograph them and leave them.

cards.title: Coyote
cards.text: Common, and heard most nights. They are wary of people but will take a small dog or cat. Keep pets close at dawn, dusk and night, and never leave food or trash out.

cards.title: Wild burros
cards.text: Burros descended from miners' pack animals live along the Colorado River between Ehrenberg and Yuma, in a herd area the BLM manages, and they wander onto US-95 south of town. Slow down at night. Do not feed them.

cards.title: Desert bighorn sheep
cards.text: The Kofa refuge was created to protect them. Scan rocky ridges and skylines early and late in the day, with binoculars.

cards.title: Mule deer
cards.text: Seen in washes at dawn and dusk, sheltering under desert trees in the heat of the day.

cards.title: Rabbits and foxes
cards.text: Black-tailed jackrabbits and desert cottontails are everywhere at dusk. Kit foxes, small with big ears, come out at night.

cards.title: Javelina
cards.text: Rare around Quartzsite. Javelina live mostly farther east and south in Arizona, and only a handful have ever been recorded in La Paz County. If you do see a group of pig-like animals, keep dogs away and give them room.

cards.title: Pack rats
cards.text: Woodrats build nests of sticks and cholla under bushes and, if they can, in engine bays, where they chew wiring. Campers who stay for weeks leave the hood up, put a light under the vehicle at night and check the engine bay often.

cards.title: Birds
cards.text: Gambel's quail in coveys, roadrunners, cactus wrens, phainopeplas, doves, hummingbirds at ocotillo and feeders, and turkey vultures and golden eagles overhead. Great horned owls call at night.

cards.title: Lizards
cards.text: Chuckwallas, desert iguanas and horned lizards bask on warm rocks from spring on. On cold winter days most stay hidden.

cards.title: Desert tortoise
cards.text: Protected, and rarely seen. Do not pick one up: a frightened tortoise can empty its bladder and lose the water it needs to survive.

cards.title: Gila monster
cards.text: A heavy orange-and-black lizard, venomous, slow and seldom seen. Leave it alone and it will leave you alone.

cards.title: Do not feed anything
cards.text: Feeding coyotes, burros or birds teaches them to come into camps and onto roads, and it usually ends badly for the animal.

cards.title: Rattlesnakes
cards.text: Western diamondbacks, sidewinders and Mojave rattlesnakes live here. In winter they are mostly underground, but they come out on warm afternoons and from March on. Watch where you put hands and feet, use a light at night and keep dogs leashed. If bitten: keep still, call 911 and get to a hospital. No cutting, sucking, ice or tourniquet.

cards.title: Scorpions
cards.text: The Arizona bark scorpion is small and pale, and its sting is the one that matters. Shake out shoes, gloves and bedding, and do not go barefoot at night. A UV flashlight makes them glow. Most stings hurt and pass. For a child, an older adult, or any trouble breathing or swallowing, call Poison Help at (800) 222-1222 or 911.

cards.title: Tarantulas
cards.text: Desert blond tarantulas live in burrows across the Sonoran Desert. You are most likely to see one in late summer and fall, when males walk about looking for mates, so winter visitors rarely do. They are slow and not dangerous. Leave them be.

cards.title: Black widows
cards.text: Glossy black with a red hourglass, in woodpiles, storage bins and under tables and chairs left outside. Wear gloves when you move things that have sat a while.

cards.title: Bees
cards.text: Wild honey bees in southern Arizona are mostly Africanized and defend a hive hard. Stay well away from any swarm or hive in a tree, rock crevice or water box. If bees come at you, run, cover your face and get inside a vehicle. Do not swat and do not jump into water.

cards.title: Cactus spines
cards.text: Tweezers take out the big ones. For the tiny hair-like ones, press on tape or let white glue dry on the skin and peel it off.

cards.title: In an emergency
cards.text: Call 911. A desert campsite has no street address, so give the GPS coordinates from your phone's map app, the nearest highway milepost and a landmark, for example "0.8 miles east of US-95 milepost 101, white Class C with a blue flag".

cards.title: Road closures
cards.text: Arizona: az511.gov. California side of I-10: quickmap.dot.ca.gov.

cards.title: Weather and county alerts
cards.text: weather.gov for wind and flash flood warnings. La Paz County alerts: lapaz.gov/AlertCenter.aspx.

cards.title: Fire restrictions and LTVA rules
cards.text: blm.gov/visit/la-posa-long-term-visitor-area. Wildfire map: inciweb.wildfire.gov.

cards.title: Border wait times
cards.text: bwt.cbp.gov, for Los Algodones (Andrade) and San Luis.

cards.title: Non-emergency numbers
cards.text: Quartzsite Police office: (928) 927-4644. Town Hall: (928) 927-4333. Poison Help: (800) 222-1222.

cards.title: County dispatch and fire district
cards.text: La Paz County dispatch: (928) 669-6141. Quartzsite Fire District: (928) 927-6556.

cards.title: La Posa South station
cards.text: Dump lanes, water faucets and trash, included with the LTVA permit. Expect lines in mid January.

cards.title: RV Pit Stop
cards.text: 425 N Central Blvd, (928) 927-3714 / (928) 380-8791. Reverse-osmosis drinking water, propane refills, ice, and RV supplies. Live status intermittently shows temporarily closed and dumping stopped in recent seasons—call ahead before pulling in.

cards.title: Tumbleweed RV Park
cards.text: 600 E Kuehn St, (928) 927-3182. About six dump lanes, usually no line. Dump $15 and water $5 when last reported.

cards.title: County transfer station
cards.text: North of town off US-95 (La Paz County Quartzsite Transfer Station). Free residential/camper trash drop-off. Winter hours (Oct 1 – Mar 31): Sun, Mon, Tue 6:00am–1:00pm (closed Wed–Sat). Call (928) 669-8886 to confirm holiday schedules.

cards.title: Flying J, Ehrenberg
cards.text: I-10 Exit 1, open 24 hours. RV dump, propane, showers and laundry.

cards.title: Blythe city RV dump
cards.text: 15901 S Broadway, Blythe. Dump on the same trip as your grocery run. The water there is not for drinking.

cards.title: RV Relief
cards.text: 918 N Central Blvd. Propane, potable water and RV dump. Seasonal hours. (928) 955-9300. rv-relief.com

cards.title: Boondocks RV Station II

cards.title: Pickleball
cards.text: Morning drop-in play is reported at the Town Park courts, all levels. Bring a paddle and outdoor balls, and come early before the wind.

cards.text: Several congregations in town hold Sunday services and free community Thanksgiving and Christmas dinners.

areas.text: Free, 14-day limit. West side of Hwy 95, about 5 miles south of town. Quieter.

pins.name: Hauser Geode Beds
pins.text: The one many visitors never hear about. On BLM land in California: take I-10 west past Blythe to the Wiley's Well Road exit, about 36 miles from Quartzsite, then go south past the Wiley's Well and Coon Hollow campgrounds to the signed dirt road. About an hour beyond Blythe, half of it on washboard dirt. Take a truck or high-clearance rig, a shovel and plenty of water.

pins.name: Red Cloud Mine
pins.text: World-famous for orange-red wulfenite, with fluorite, willemite and calcite that glow under UV. You pay to dig the tailings. The 2026/27 season opened September 18. See redcloudmine.com before you drive.

pins.name: Opal Hill Mine
pins.text: Fire agate site in the Mule Mountains, near Coon Hollow campground off Wiley's Well Road. Visitors describe a pay-to-dig mine open in the cool season, reached by a high-clearance 4WD road. Find out whether it is open before you drive.

pins.name: Saddle Mountain
pins.text: BLM land near Tonopah, about 80 miles east on I-10, with petroglyphs, hiking, rockhounding and free 14-day camping. The dirt roads in are rough in places.

pins.name: Big Bertha Mine
pins.text: Old mine and hiking area in the Dome Rock Mountains west of town.

pins.name: Wyatt Earp's Mine
pins.text: A small historic mine in the hills on the California side of the river, north-west of Parker. Visitors say you need a 4WD, or a walk up a sandy wash, to reach it.

pins.name: Agate and Palm Mine
pins.text: Far out in the desert north of Wenden, off Alamo Lake Road and a long dirt road. One visitor reports green onyx and palm bog in the wash and flats beside the mine.

pins.name: Quartzsite Town Park
pins.text: By the library on Plymouth Ave, open 7am to 9pm. Visitors describe a splash pad, disc golf and a skate park. Reported to have restrooms, shaded picnic ramadas, pickleball and basketball courts, walking paths and a playground. A daytime stop when you need shade.

pins.name: Quartzsite Dog Park
pins.text: A fenced off-leash area at 555 Plymouth Rd, next to Town Park, open 6am to 6pm, with separate sides for large and small dogs. Safer than the open desert, away from cholla and coyotes.

pins.name: Reader's Oasis Books
pins.text: 690 E Main St. The well-known roadside used bookstore. It may not keep regular hours, so check before you go.

pins.name: Holiday Palms RV Park
pins.text: 355 W Main St, (928) 927-5666. Pool, dances, exercise classes and pickleball. Not staying there? Call the office and ask about day use.

pins.name: Quartzsite Community & Senior Center
pins.text: 295 E Chandler St, (928) 927-4333 ext. 404. Open Mon 7:00am–6:00pm, Tue–Thu 7:00am–2:30pm (closed 12–1pm; closed Fri–Sun). Hosts senior congregate meals, card games, fitness classes, and seasonal town events.

pins.name: Palm Canyon, Kofa refuge
pins.text: Arizona's only native palms, about 45 California fan palms in a narrow gorge. Drive 19 miles south on Hwy 95, then about 7 miles east on Palm Canyon Road to the trailhead. It is about a half-mile walk to the overlook. A passenger car is fine in good weather. No water or services.

pins.name: The Desert Bar, Parker
pins.text: The Nellie E Saloon: an off-grid, solar-powered Old West bar in the Buckskin Mountains, 5 miles down rough Cienega Springs Road off Hwy 95 north of Parker. Reported hours are Saturday and Sunday, noon to 6, from about early October to late April, with live music most weekends. Families and pets welcome. High clearance recommended. (928) 667-2871.

pins.name: Cibola National Wildlife Refuge
pins.text: About 45 miles southwest (via I-10 west to Blythe, then south along the Colorado River on Neighbours Blvd / Cibola Lake Rd). Prime winter birdwatching for tens of thousands of sandhill cranes, Canada geese, snow geese, and raptors along the auto tour loop (Nov–Feb).

pins.name: Yuma Territorial Prison & Historic Downtown
pins.text: About 85 miles south via US-95. Tour the 1876 sandstone prison cells overlooking the Colorado River, walk the historic Main Street shops and restaurants, or combine with a morning walk across to Los Algodones.

pins.name: Imperial National Wildlife Refuge
pins.text: About 65 miles south off US-95. Free. Colorado River wetlands, wildlife lookouts and the short Painted Desert Trail. Visitor center reported open Friday to Sunday, 10 to 4, in winter.

pins.name: Bill Williams River National Wildlife Refuge
pins.text: About 45 miles north, just past Parker. Birdwatching, level viewing areas and flat-water paddling where the river meets Lake Havasu.

pins.name: Poston Memorial Monument
pins.text: About 30 miles north near Poston. A free roadside monument to the Poston War Relocation Center, where more than 17,000 Japanese Americans were held in World War II. Paved pull-off with plaques.

pins.name: Buckskin Mountain and River Island state parks
pins.text: About 47 miles north on the Parker Strip. Riverside picnic spots, paved walks, a beach and hiking trails. azstateparks.com.

pins.name: Parker Dam
pins.text: About 50 miles north. A scenic river drive on AZ-95 to the dam overlook.

pins.name: Alamo Lake State Park
pins.text: A remote desert lake northeast of town for fishing and kayaking. A long drive; fuel up first.

pins.name: Tyson Wash petroglyphs and grinding holes
pins.text: Just south of town off Hwy 95. Park before Tyson Wash; the petroglyphs are on a rocky outcrop, with caves and grinding holes on the cliff across the wash. GPS 33.61566, -114.237724.

pins.name: Clapp Spring
pins.text: A desert spring in the Palo Verde Mountains south of Coon Hollow, known to rockhounds for the tube agate nearby. Do not count on finding water there.

pins.name: Livingston Hills
pins.text: Low hills a few miles south of Crystal Hill, off US-95 south of Quartzsite.

pins.name: Walter's Wash
pins.text: A small nature preserve near Roll, north-east of Yuma. A long day trip south.

pins.name: RV Pit Stop
pins.text: 425 N Central Blvd, (928) 927-3714 / (928) 380-8791. Reverse-osmosis drinking water, propane refills, ice, and RV supplies. Live status intermittently shows temporarily closed and dumping stopped in recent seasons—call ahead before pulling in.

pins.name: Tumbleweed RV Park
pins.text: 600 E Kuehn St, (928) 927-3182. About six dump lanes, usually no line. Dump $15 and water $5 when last reported.

pins.text: North of town off US-95 (La Paz County Quartzsite Transfer Station). Free residential/camper trash drop-off. Winter hours (Oct 1 – Mar 31): Sun, Mon, Tue 6:00am–1:00pm (closed Wed–Sat). Call (928) 669-8886 to confirm holiday schedules.

pins.text: 615 W Main St.

pins.name: Southern Tire Mart at Pilot
pins.text: 1141 W Main St. Truck tires. Ask about RV sizes.

pins.name: Jessie's Tire Service, Blythe
pins.text: 1518 E Hobsonway. Cars, trucks, RVs and ATVs. Open evenings and Sundays.

pins.name: Joe's Tires, Blythe
pins.text: 1126 E Hobsonway. Tires, alignments and brakes.

pins.name: Standage Tire & Auto (Goodyear), Blythe
pins.text: 418 W Hobsonway. Also has an Ehrenberg shop.

pins.name: Alex Tire Sales, Blythe
pins.text: 1340 W Hobsonway. Carries Firestone.

pins.name: Best Auto RV & Truck Repair
pins.text: 585 N Central Blvd, (928) 927-8787. Weekdays 8 to 5.

pins.name: Mead Automotive and RV Repair, Blythe
Split Rail Recreational Sales and Rentals
pins.text: Split Rail RV Park, 1258 N Central Blvd. Needs 24 hours' notice. (928) 927-5296.

pins.name: Gem World
pins.text: 1330 W Main St, (626) 922-1258. Open daily 10:00am–5:00pm year-round. Gems, rough rock, beads, and lapidary/jewelry supplies (wholesale and retail).

pins.name: Coyote Fresh Foods
pins.text: 410 E Main St. Open daily 7:00am–7:00pm. Popular local stop praised by campers for quality fresh meats, deli items, and quick grocery runs without driving to Blythe.

pins.name: Roadrunner Market
pins.text: 200 E Main St. Open daily 8:00am–7:00pm. Largest full-service grocery in town (a couple blocks east of US-95) with fresh produce, meat, staples, and liquor.

pins.name: Ace Hardware, Blythe
pins.text: The nearest full hardware store, 20 miles west on I-10.

pins.name: Big Market
pins.text: 775 W Main St, (928) 927-5432. Open daily 8:00am–6:00pm. Hardware, tools, RV basics, groceries, and liquor in town. Convenience pricing runs higher than Blythe.

pins.name: Main Street Laundromat
pins.text: 205 E Main St. (928) 927-4163. Washers from about $2.50, dryers a quarter per five minutes, showers about $11 for 20 minutes when last reported. Open 6:00am to 4:30pm.

pins.name: Post Office
pins.text: 80 W Main St, (928) 927-6323. Retail/pickup counter open Mon–Fri 9:00am–11:00am and 12:00pm–4:00pm (closed for lunch 11am–12pm; closed Sat–Sun). PO Box lobby open Mon–Sat 6:00am–6:00pm. General Delivery held 30 days; expect long lines in Jan–Feb.

pins.name: BCM Mail & Ship
pins.text: 852 W Cowell St, (928) 927-4213. Mailboxes.

pins.name: FedEx at Dollar General
pins.text: 925 W Main. Pick up and drop off FedEx packages.

pins.name: IMS Urgent Care
pins.text: 255 N Central Blvd, Suite 7. Walk-ins.

pins.name: La Paz Regional Hospital, Parker
pins.text: Emergency room, plus urgent care on weekdays.

pins.name: Happy Valley Pharmacy
pins.text: 60 W Main St. Rumors of closing come up in the groups, so call ahead. Walmart in Parker has a pharmacy.

pins.name: Smile Bright Dental
pins.text: 301 E Hobsonway, (760) 922-2300. Listed as taking new patients.

pins.name: Dr. Tiffany Wade
pins.text: 146 S Broadway, (760) 922-8144. Listed as taking new patients.

pins.name: Dr. Eric Clark
pins.text: 500 N Broadway, Suite 4, (760) 922-0266.

pins.name: Innercare Blythe Dental
pins.text: 1415 W Hobsonway, (760) 922-4981. Community health center. Ask about fees without insurance.

pins.name: Pristine Dental Hygiene
pins.text: 115 E Hobsonway, (760) 922-5320. Cleanings.

pins.name: Novak Animal Care Center, Lake Havasu City
pins.text: 332 London Bridge Rd, (928) 855-0588.

pins.name: QIA
pins.text: 235 E Ironwood St. Beyond the Pow Wow and the theater, members report lapidary and stained glass workshops, line dancing, yoga, pancake breakfasts and potlucks. Winter visitors can join.

pins.name: Quartzsite Food Bank
pins.text: 40 N Moon Mountain Ave, (928) 662-7000. Winter hours Tuesday and Thursday, 8am to noon. fqfoodbank.com.

pins.name: Salvation Army thrift store
pins.text: 101 Moon Mountain Ave, (928) 927-3636. Secondhand clothes, blankets and kitchenware, plus referrals for emergency help.

pins.name: Nikki's Nook, Bouse
pins.text: 28332 Hwy 72, about 25 miles north. A free thrift store and food pantry, reported open Saturday 11 to 3.

pins.name: Silly Al's Pizza
pins.text: 175 W Main St, (928) 927-5585. Longtime Quartzsite pizza place: specialty pizzas, wings and cold beer, with big crowds in show season.

pins.name: Mountain Quail Cafe
pins.text: 500 N Moon Mountain Ave, (928) 927-8890. Open daily 7:00am–7:00pm. Sit-down diner favorite for hearty breakfasts, burgers, and classic comfort food.
